setup: Set the thigh pad snug on top of your thighs
Grip a little wider than your shoulders
Sit tall, chest up, slight lean back
execution: Pull your elbows down toward your ribs
Bring the bar to your upper chest
Keep your chest up; don't swing back
Let the bar rise slowly to straight arms
faults: Don't pull the bar behind your neck
Don't lean far back and swing
Don't shrug your shoulders toward your ears
Don't let the stack yank your arms up

notes: Pull to the front of the face, not behind the neck.
Return the bar under control so it doesn't drop toward your head.
Keep hold of the bar as you stand up, then let it rise slowly. Don't let go at the top.
If pain lingers or comes back, stop this exercise and get it checked by a physio or doctor.
stopIf: Pain that changes how you move

regressions.name: Single-arm pulldown
regressions.reason: One arm at a time with a lighter load; easier to feel the elbow path.

progressions.name: Assisted pull-up
progressions.reason: Moves the same pull onto your own bodyweight, with help.

progressions.name: Pull-up
progressions.reason: Same vertical pull with bodyweight as the load.

substitutions.name: Assisted pull-up
substitutions.reason: Same vertical pull. Load is assistance: a larger number is easier.

substitutions.name: Pull-up
substitutions.reason: Same vertical pull with no machine.

substitutions.name: Neutral-grip pulldown
substitutions.reason: Same machine with a different handle; some people find it more comfortable.

substitutions.reason: Lats with little biceps work; isolation.

substitutions.name: One-arm dumbbell row

guideBrief.cameraNote: Front view, figure facing the camera, seated, camera at chest height. Pulley and cable directly above the centre of the bar. Seat and thigh pads visible; the weight stack is optional, behind the figure.

keyPositions.label: Start
keyPositions.describe: Seated, thighs under the pads, feet flat, knees about 90°. Arms reaching up in a wide V, hands on the bar about 1.5× shoulder width with an overhand grip. Elbows almost straight, shoulders allowed to rise slightly.

keyPositions.label: Halfway
keyPositions.describe: Bar at about eye level, moving straight down in front of the face. Elbows bending and travelling down and out. Shoulders have moved down.

keyPositions.label: Bottom
keyPositions.describe: Bar at the upper chest, just below the chin. Elbows down beside the ribs, roughly under the hands, forearms close to vertical. Shoulders down and back, chest up.

ikHints: Hands fixed to the bar at about 1.5× shoulder width
Bar centre on the body's midline, moving vertically from overhead to upper-chest height
Hips fixed on the seat; thighs under the pads; feet planted
guideBrief.barPath: Straight down and up along the body's midline; cable stays vertical from the bar centre to the pulley
emphasise: Elbows drive down toward the ribs
Bar finishes at the upper chest, in front of the face
Shoulders move down as the pull starts

sources.title: Lusk SJ, Hale BD, Russell DM (2010) Grip width and forearm orientation effects on muscle activity during the lat pull-down. J Strength Cond Res 24(7):1895-1900
Mike Reinold: The Lat Pulldown – How to Maximize Latissimus Activity
Mayo Clinic video: Lat pull-down with weight machine

uncertain.note: Front-view elbow angle is a 2D projection. With the elbows partly in front of the body, the true elbow bend is smaller than it looks from the front. The guide-maker should use IK (hands on the bar at upper-chest height, elbows under the hands) rather than these numbers.
Sources differ: Reinold advises an upright spine, while a slight lean back is common gym practice. Neither gives an angle. A front view can't show the lean anyway, so it is cued in text only.
